approvalScope: Teacher explicitly approved Q55 local stagnation-point and Q56 large-reservoir negligible-speed separate self-practice variants and B/B original answer letters on 2026-11-23, withholding all individual formal scientific/SLO/cognitive/exam certification.

replacements.originalStem: If ideal horizontal water slows from 4 m/s to 0 m/s, by how much does static pressure increase?
replacements.proposedStem: In steady ideal horizontal flow, water of density 1000 kg/m³ moves at 4 m/s at point X and reaches a stagnation point Y (local speed 0 m/s) along the same streamline. Neglect viscous losses. By how much is the static pressure at Y greater than at X?
replacements.explanation: Along a horizontal, lossless streamline ending at a stagnation point, P_Y − P_X = ½ρ(v_X² − v_Y²) = ½(1000)(4² − 0²) = 8000 Pa = 8 kPa. The original answer B is correct when the zero-speed condition is local stagnation, not zero discharge everywhere.
replacements.sourceProvenance: Teacher-prepared original from compiled master pp.189-190; revised stem is teacher-approved pedagogical adaptation, not a verbatim NBF question.
replacements.scientificModelWarning: Local stagnation point only; no claim all flow in a finite pipe stops

replacements.originalStem: Ideal horizontal water accelerates from rest to 10 m/s. If upstream pressure is 100 kPa, the downstream pressure is:
replacements.proposedStem: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ flows steadily from a very large reservoir into a horizontal duct. At point X in the reservoir, its speed is negligible and its static pressure is 100 kPa. At point Y downstream on the same elevation and streamline, the water speed is 10 m/s. Neglect viscous losses and pumps. What is the static pressure at Y?
replacements.explanation: Apply ideal horizontal Bernoulli between a near-stagnant point in a very large reservoir and a downstream point on the same streamline. P_Y = P_X + ½ρ(v_X² − v_Y²) ≈ 100000 + ½(1000)(0 − 10²) Pa = 50000 Pa = 50 kPa. The original letter B is retained. No downstream atmospheric discharge is assumed.
